promptText: Why is Map intentionally NOT a sub-interface of Collection, even though both live in the Collections Framework?
options: A Collection stores individual elements while a Map stores key-value pairs, so the two have fundamentally incompatible contracts and sit in separate hierarchies
Map was added in a later Java version than Collection and the two were never reconciled for backward-compatibility reasons
Map cannot support generics, unlike List, Set, and Queue which all extend Collection
Extending Collection would make Map's keys allow duplicates, which violates Map's contract
explanation: List, Set, and Queue all extend Collection because they hold single elements with element-based operations (add, remove, iterate); Map's core operation is associating a key with a value, an entirely different shape of contract, which is why it deliberately sits in its own hierarchy rather than forcing an awkward fit.

promptText: A HashMap is described as having O(1) average-case lookup. Which statement correctly qualifies this claim?
options: The O(1) average assumes a well-distributed hashCode(); heavy collisions degrade a bucket toward O(log n) after Java 8 treeification, or O(n) in a naive linked-list bucket
O(1) is guaranteed in every case, because HashMap always converts every bucket into a balanced tree regardless of size
HashMap is actually O(log n) on average because every get() must traverse the internal red-black tree
The O(1) guarantee only applies to put(), never to get()
explanation: HashMap's speed depends entirely on hash quality: a poor hashCode() (e.g. one that always returns a constant) collapses many keys into one bucket, and before Java 8 that bucket was a plain linked list scanned in O(n); Java 8's treeification of large buckets caps the worst case at O(log n), but the O(1) figure is always an average, not a guarantee.

promptText: Why does HashMap special-case a null key by assigning it to bucket 0, rather than computing its bucket the normal way?
options: Calling hashCode() on a null reference would throw a NullPointerException, so HashMap bypasses the hash calculation entirely for the null key
Null keys are hashed using the identity hash of the HashMap instance itself
HashMap forbids null keys entirely, exactly like Hashtable and ConcurrentHashMap
Bucket 0 is reserved specifically so that null keys sort first during iteration
explanation: Because null.hashCode() would throw an NPE, HashMap treats the null key as a special case and stores it directly in bucket 0 rather than attempting to hash it; this is a deliberate convenience unique to HashMap, since Hashtable and ConcurrentHashMap forbid null keys/values entirely to avoid ambiguity.

promptText: HashSet is described internally as "just a HashMap." What does adding an element to a HashSet actually do under the hood?
options: It calls put() on a backing HashMap, using the element as the key and a shared dummy constant as the value, so uniqueness is enforced entirely by the map's own key-collision logic
It appends the element to an internal ArrayList and then removes duplicates in a separate pass
It stores the element's hashCode as the value and the element itself as an array index
It maintains a separate sorted tree purely for duplicate detection, independent of any Map
explanation: HashSet is a thin wrapper: add() delegates to the backing HashMap's put(where the value is a single shared dummy object), so it inherits all of HashMap's hashing, collision-handling, and equals/hashCode reliance rather than reimplementing uniqueness checking itself.

promptText: The Queue interface offers offer()/poll()/peek() alongside add()/remove()/element(). What is the functional difference between these two method families?
options: offer(), poll(), and peek() return a special value (false or null) when the operation cannot be performed; add(), remove(), and element() throw an exception instead
offer(), poll(), and peek() are deprecated aliases for add(), remove(), and element()
add(), remove(), and element() only work on bounded queues, while offer(), poll(), and peek() only work on unbounded queues
offer() inserts at the tail while add() inserts at the head of the queue
explanation: Both families do the same conceptual work, but they differ in how they signal failure on an empty or full queue: the non-throwing family (offer/poll/peek) is generally preferred in production because it allows handling an edge case through normal control flow instead of exception handling.

promptText: With HashMap's default load factor of 0.75 and an initial capacity of 16, after how many entries does the map trigger a resize?
options: After the 12th entry is inserted (16 * 0.75 = 12), the next insertion triggers a resize
After exactly 16 entries, once the table is completely full
After 8 entries, since load factor doubles the effective threshold
Resize only happens when a single bucket exceeds 8 entries, regardless of total size
explanation: The resize threshold is capacity multiplied by load factor: 16 * 0.75 = 12, so the map resizes (doubling capacity and rehashing every entry) once its size would exceed 12, not when the raw array slots are literally full or based on a single bucket's size alone.

promptText: LinkedList can theoretically insert/remove in O(1), yet ArrayList is used far more often in practice for general-purpose lists. Why does LinkedList's insertion advantage rarely materialize?
options: Reaching the insertion point in a LinkedList still costs O(n) traversal unless you already hold a positioned iterator, and its scattered nodes cause more cache misses than ArrayList's contiguous, cache-friendly array
LinkedList does not actually support insertion or removal at arbitrary positions, only at the head and tail
ArrayList's insertions are always O(1) even in the middle, making LinkedList strictly worse in every case
JVMs no longer implement LinkedList as a true linked structure, so its theoretical complexity claims are outdated
explanation: The O(1) splice only applies once you're already positioned at the right node; getting there from an index is O(n), and each node's scattered memory location causes more cache misses than ArrayList's contiguous array, which is why ArrayList tends to win in real workloads even where Big-O superficially favors LinkedList.

promptText: What specific change did Java 8 make to how HashMap handles a bucket with many colliding entries, and what triggers it?
options: Once a bucket exceeds a treeify threshold of 8 entries (with the table at least 64 in size), that bucket's linked list is converted into a red-black tree, improving worst-case lookup from O(n) to O(log n); it reverts to a list if the bucket later shrinks
Java 8 removed collision handling entirely and instead grows the whole table by 4x whenever any collision occurs
Java 8 caps every bucket at exactly 8 entries and silently drops any entry beyond that limit
Java 8 replaced linked-list buckets with a secondary HashMap nested inside each bucket
explanation: Before Java 8, a pathological hashCode() could collapse a HashMap's performance to O(n) linear scans within one bucket; treeification specifically targets buckets that grow past the threshold (and only once the table itself is large enough), converting just that bucket into a balanced tree rather than changing the whole table's structure.

promptText: Why does ConcurrentHashMap forbid null keys and null values, while HashMap permits one null key?
options: A null return from get() would be ambiguous under concurrency ("key absent" vs "key present with null value"), and another thread could change the map between a get() and a disambiguating containsKey() check, so ConcurrentHashMap removes the ambiguity by disallowing null entirely
ConcurrentHashMap's internal array uses null internally as a sentinel marking an empty bucket, so a null key or value would corrupt that bookkeeping
This restriction is simply a historical accident with no design rationale behind it
Null values would force ConcurrentHashMap to acquire a global lock on every read, defeating its performance goals
explanation: In a single-threaded HashMap you can safely disambiguate a null result with containsKey(), but in a concurrent map another thread could insert or remove the key between the two calls, making that check unreliable; forbidding null entirely means a null return can only ever mean "absent," keeping the contract safe under concurrency.

promptText: In `for(String s : list){ list.add("Java"); }` on an ArrayList, what actually causes the ConcurrentModificationException, and is this strictly a multi-threading issue?
options: The iterator tracks a modCount snapshot at creation; each next() call checks it against the list's current modCount, and add() inside the loop changes that count, so the mismatch is detected -- this happens even on a single thread, so the exception name is somewhat misleading
The exception only occurs because two separate threads are both iterating the same list concurrently
ArrayList physically locks itself during iteration, and add() blocks until the loop finishes, never actually throwing an exception
The exception is thrown by the garbage collector when it detects the list resizing mid-iteration
explanation: Fail-fast behavior is driven by a simple modCount check inside the iterator, not by any multi-threading detection; structurally modifying the list via the list itself (rather than the iterator's own remove()) invalidates that count and trips the check on the very next call to next(), regardless of whether a second thread is even involved.

promptText: A PriorityQueue is implemented as a binary heap. What guarantee does this structure actually provide, and what common assumption about it is wrong?
options: It guarantees only that the head (poll()/peek()) is the smallest/highest-priority element; iterating the queue directly does NOT yield elements in fully sorted order
It guarantees the entire queue is always in fully sorted order when iterated, just like a TreeSet
It guarantees O(1) insertion and O(1) removal of the head, unlike a sorted list
It guarantees that ties in priority are broken by insertion order, similar to a stable sort
explanation: A binary heap only maintains the heap property (each parent is <= its children in a min-heap), which is enough to make the head always the smallest element, but the rest of the array is not fully ordered -- a common trap for candidates who assume iterating a PriorityQueue produces sorted output; insert and remove of the head both cost O(log n), not O(1).

promptText: Between HashMap and TreeMap, what is the actual trade-off being made, and which one permits a null key?
options: HashMap gives average O(1) access with no ordering guarantee and allows one null key; TreeMap guarantees sorted order (and range queries like floorKey/ceilingKey) at O(log n) per operation but rejects null keys because every key must be compared to position it in the tree
TreeMap is strictly faster than HashMap because its red-black tree avoids hash collisions entirely
Both permit null keys, but only TreeMap permits null values
HashMap maintains insertion order while TreeMap maintains natural ordering; both have identical O(log n) performance
explanation: The core trade-off is ordering versus raw speed: HashMap trades any ordering guarantee for average constant-time operations, while TreeMap's red-black tree keeps keys continuously sorted at the cost of logarithmic time, and because positioning a key requires comparing it, a null key (which can't be compared) is rejected outright.

promptText: How did ConcurrentHashMap's internal locking strategy fundamentally change between Java 7 and Java 8+, and why does this matter for a candidate's answer?
options: Java 7 divided the map into a fixed number of independently-locked segments (16 by default), capping concurrency at the segment count; Java 8+ replaced this with per-bucket locking using CAS for empty buckets and synchronization only on a bucket's first node during a collision, with reads generally lock-free -- most candidates still describe only the outdated Java 7 model
Java 7 had no internal locking at all and relied entirely on the JVM's garbage collector for safety, while Java 8 introduced the first locking mechanism
Java 8 removed all concurrency support and now requires external synchronization identical to a plain HashMap
Both versions use identical segment-based locking; the only Java 8 change was renaming 'segments' to 'buckets' in the source code
explanation: Java 7's fixed 16 segments meant only 16 threads could write concurrently without contention; Java 8 pushed lock granularity down to individual buckets (CAS for the common case, synchronized only on genuine collisions), which is a materially finer-grained and higher-throughput design -- explaining this Java 8 shift instead of the legacy segment model is explicitly called out as a way to stand out in an interview.

promptText: You call `new HashMap<>(1000)` expecting to insert exactly 1000 elements without any resize. Why might a resize still occur before the 1000th insertion?
options: The constructor argument sets the initial bucket-array size, but the resize threshold is still capacity * 0.75 (load factor); to truly avoid any resize while loading 1000 elements you must size for roughly 1000 / 0.75, not just pass 1000 directly
The constructor argument is silently ignored by the JVM in all Java versions, so the map always starts at the default capacity of 16
HashMap resizes exactly once after every 100 insertions regardless of the constructor argument
Passing an initial capacity disables load-factor-based resizing entirely, so no resize would ever occur in this scenario
explanation: The constructor argument only sets the starting bucket-array size; the 0.75 default load factor still applies on top of it, so a map sized for exactly 1000 will hit its resize threshold (750) well before reaching 1000 entries -- the subtlety senior engineers know is to divide the expected size by the load factor when pre-sizing to genuinely avoid any resize during a bulk load.

promptText: Beyond simple lost updates, what was the more severe historical danger of sharing a plain (pre-fix) HashMap across multiple threads during a resize, and what is the recommended fix?
options: Concurrent structural modification during resize could corrupt the linked-list rehashing logic into forming a cycle, causing an infinite loop that pegs a CPU core at 100%; the fix is to use ConcurrentHashMap (or externally synchronize) rather than share a plain HashMap across threads
The JVM would silently convert the HashMap into a TreeMap to protect itself, permanently changing its performance characteristics
The map would automatically become read-only after detecting the first concurrent write, blocking all future put() calls
Resize failures under concurrency only ever throw a catchable ConcurrentModificationException, with no other risk
explanation: Beyond ordinary lost updates from unsynchronized writes, older JVM versions had a well-documented bug where concurrent resizing could corrupt a bucket's linked list into a cycle, causing get() or put() to spin forever and consume 100% CPU on a core -- a stronger, more concrete argument for ConcurrentHashMap than merely citing 'thread safety' in the abstract.
